statement: Three friends choose seats in a row of 7 empty chairs so that no two of them sit next to each other. In how many different ways can they do this, if it matters who sits where?

choices.misconception: I counted which three chairs are used but forgot the three friends can swap among those chairs.
I counted all seatings of three people in 7 chairs and ignored the rule about sitting next to each other.
I counted sets of three chairs without the rule and without arranging the friends.
I only removed the seatings where all three sit together, not those where just two are side by side.

hints: First decide which chairs are used, then who sits where.
Choose the set of chairs first, keeping gaps between them, and only afterwards place the three friends. A neat way to count gapped chairs is to remove the compulsory empty chairs between friends.
Between the friends there must be at least one empty chair in each of the two gaps. Take those 2 chairs away and choose any 3 of the remaining 5.

solutions.reliable: Listing the chair sets with gaps, written as chair numbers: 135, 136, 137, 146, 147, 157, 246, 247, 257, 357 gives 10 sets. In each set the three friends can be arranged in 3 times 2 times 1 = 6 ways, so there are 60 seatings. The transferable idea: in restricted counting, choose the positions under the rule first and arrange the people afterwards.
solutions.elegant: Remove one empty chair from each of the two gaps that must exist; any choice of 3 of the remaining 5 chairs then corresponds to exactly one gapped choice in the original row, so there are 10 chair sets and 10 times 6 = 60 seatings. The transferable idea: squeeze out the forced gaps to turn a restricted count into an unrestricted one.

whyOnTest: Counting with a 'not next to each other' rule tests whether you separate choosing places from arranging people and handle every forbidden case.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
